title: PRISM
tagline: Privileged-user Risk Identification and Surveillance Monitoring
summary: Real-time insider-fraud detection for banking staff — a graph network and behavioral ensemble fused via Dempster-Shafer, cutting false positives 60-70% and investigation time to minutes.
description: PRISM is a real-time early-warning system for insider fraud at Union Bank of India, built for the PSBs' IDEA 2.0 Hackathon. Two employees colluding never trip a single-user rule; a compromised login looks identical to a real one until it's too late; slow, gradual privilege creep rarely crosses any static threshold. PRISM cross-references relationship, behavioral, and session-level evidence and only alerts when multiple independent signals agree — cutting false positives by 60-70% and mean investigation time from 4-6 hours to 12 minutes.

The pipeline runs as two independent detection layers fused into one verdict. Layer 1 is a graph attention network that scores the bank's entire employee/customer/account relationship graph — cached in memory so every read is instant — paired with Louvain community detection to surface collusion rings and hidden beneficiaries that look clean in isolation. Layer 2 is a stacking ensemble (XGBoost + LightGBM + Isolation Forest into a logistic-regression meta-learner) over 30+ engineered behavioral features per employee — off-hours activity, transaction velocity, dormant-account access, privilege changes, new-device logins — trained with SMOTE to handle a fraud rate under 1%.

A Dempster-Shafer fusion engine combines the two layers' belief masses rather than averaging their scores: it preserves uncertainty instead of hiding it, and a conflict score surfaces disagreement for human review instead of guessing. When both layers independently flag the same employee the combined score amplifies well past either one alone — in one worked case, individual scores of 0.72 and 0.83 fused to 0.947 with a conflict score of just 0.097, a confident, low-conflict CRITICAL alert.

Every alert explains itself. SHAP ranks each prediction's feature contributions and a narrative generator turns them into a plain-English causal chain — "3 off-hours transactions, 2 transfers to a dependent account, cross-branch access from 2 new IPs, transaction count 4.2x above average" — plus 15 boolean risk signals (premature FD breaks, limit overrides, bulk data exports, repeated failed logins, and more) investigators can act on directly instead of reverse-engineering a black-box score.
## Dataset

A synthetic Union Bank dataset was built for training and demo: 73,669 records across 7 MongoDB collections — 400 employees, 2,000 customers, 3,837 accounts, 21,785 transactions, 45,382 activity logs, and 665 dependents over a 6-month window — with 12 injected fraud scenario types (collusion rings, FD premature-breaks, dormant-account activity, bulk data exports, repeated failed logins, and more) fully labelled for supervised training and evaluation.
## Product

Three role-aware dashboards — Admin/Fraud Analyst, Branch Manager, and Employee self-service — are built in Next.js with a live alert feed, a relationship graph, a What-If simulator, JWT/RBAC access control, and the UI localized into 10 Indian languages. All three ML services — the graph network, the behavioral ensemble, and the fusion orchestrator — run as independently scaled FastAPI microservices on Google Cloud Run against a shared MongoDB store, so every model sees exactly the data the app writes.

title: Raseed
tagline: Agentic Receipt Management for Google Wallet

galleryCaptions./images/projects/raseed/UI-Add-receipt.p: Add a receipt — scan, upload, or dictate

summary: AI-powered receipt and financial assistant integrated with Google Wallet, with agentic recipe and tax-reimbursement helpers.
description: RASEED is an AI-powered receipt and financial assistant integrated with Google Wallet. It turns everyday transactions into structured, queryable records and actionable financial guidance — receipt ingestion, budgeting, and spending insights, plus recurring-payment tracking, family mode, recipe generation, and tax assistance, all powered by Gemini models and Vertex AI.

Receipts come in three ways: photograph or upload them and Gemini extracts the metadata, dictate the purchase by voice, or type it directly into the entry form. A cloud function then classifies each item as recurring, warranty, or food based on database triggers, routing it into the right table automatically.

Confirmed receipts can be pushed straight to Google Wallet as a custom pass — built on generic-pass classes per receipt category, with hero images and color coding, text and link modules carrying metadata on the back of the pass, and a deep link back into the app.

Recurring items get tracked against their own deadlines, with reminders sent as a payment approaches; warranty items are tracked the same way, either parsed straight from the receipt or added manually against a specific item.

Spending is broken down into categories — Groceries, Entertainment, and the rest — with per-category budget limits, over-budget flags, and a custom date range for reviewing any window of activity. Family mode extends the same view across a household: add members by email and see joint analytics across the same curated categories.
## Agents

A recipe generator agent proposes recipes from the food items a user has actually bought, respecting whatever dietary restrictions or time constraints are given. It pulls from a database-access tool and a Google Search tool, merges the two through a combining agent, and runs the result through a validator agent that checks instructions were followed and keeps hallucination in check.

A tax and reimbursement agent does two things: a Vertex AI tool classifies every receipt into a fixed set of categories and totals the indirect tax paid per category, while a Firestore tool surfaces which receipts are eligible for reimbursement based on their category and subcategory.
## Future scope

Planned next: ML-driven spending analysis that predicts expenditure patterns and nudges budgets before a category runs over — down to context-aware suggestions like recommending a bus over a cab when a travel allowance is running low. Google Pay auto-ingestion, registering RASEED as a share-target app so a shared GPay receipt gets parsed and tagged with zero manual entry. And context-aware purchase recommendations, where a chatbot query like "I want to buy paneer tikka" returns ranked options across price, proximity, offers, and sustainability.

title: Job Hunter
tagline: Agentic Job Discovery Pipeline for Indian Tech Roles

galleryCaptions./images/projects/jobhunter/jobhunter-job: Filterable job list — city, YOE, source, region
galleryCaptions./images/projects/jobhunter/jobhunter-cra: Crawl run history — sources, jobs found, errors
galleryCaptions./images/projects/jobhunter/jobhunter-rej: Rejected postings, grouped by filter reason

summary: A LangGraph crawl pipeline plus a FastAPI/Next.js dashboard that discovers and filters entry-level tech jobs across 498 Indian and remote ATS sources.
description: Job Hunter is a personal job-discovery pipeline built to surface entry-level SDE/Data/ML/Cloud roles that generic job boards bury, with a deliberate tilt toward Indian startups, mid-size companies, and remote-friendly roles over large enterprises. A LangGraph agent pipeline crawls ATS boards and remote-job aggregators directly, normalizes and filters postings, validates them with Gemini, and persists them to Postgres; a read-only FastAPI service and a Next.js dashboard sit on top for browsing and filtering the results.

Getting from a handful of hand-picked companies to 498 real, working sources happened in layers: seeding known Indian companies and static aggregator feeds, then discovery passes that only ever insert a source after a live probe actually returns a real job list — YC's public hiring feed (filtered by tech tags or an India/South Asia region match), a directory of roughly 15,700 Indian company names pulled from cutshort.io's public sitemap (its job-listing pages are off-limits per robots.txt, but the sitemap is explicitly allowed for crawling), and funding-announcement RSS parsing. A dozen ATS platforms are supported — Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, SmartRecruiters, Workable, Recruitee, Breezy, Personio, and Keka (reverse-engineered from a careers page's inline JS, since it has no public docs) — plus five aggregator feeds.

Each posting runs through a five-node pipeline: fetch, normalize into a canonical shape, a deterministic keyword filter that skips the LLM entirely on obvious non-matches, a Gemini cross-check that validates and classifies what's left, then persist. Rejected postings aren't dropped — they're annotated with why and kept, so filter tuning happens against real stored data instead of a blind, crawl-expensive loop. A post-crawl enrichment agent then sweeps the whole table for anything still ambiguous, resolving experience level deterministically from stated years-of-experience where possible and falling back to a Gemini call with an explicit rubric and a required evidence field — with an asymmetric forcing rule: an unresolved posting defaults toward visibility rather than being hidden, since a wrongly-shown mid-level role costs 30 seconds of reading but a wrongly-hidden entry-level one costs an application you were eligible for.
## Performance

The crawl originally ran one source at a time in a plain sequential loop, despite being almost entirely I/O-bound. Rebuilt as a LangGraph fan-out using the Send API — one isolated sub-graph per source, bounded concurrency, a reducer for the shared results list — and benchmarked head-to-head against the old code rather than assumed: sources with no relevant postings (no LLM call at all) came back 5.76x faster, and a full 498-source production crawl dropped from 37m 26s to 4m 34s, a genuine ~8x improvement, verified end-to-end with zero fetch errors.
## Real bugs, found running against live data

Job postings were quietly duplicating on every re-crawl. The dedup key had been treated as enforced since the start but never actually was — the one real uniqueness constraint missed a live case where a single ATS tenant had posted six byte-identical listings under six different IDs in one crawl. Fixed at the application layer, deleting any other row sharing that content's hash after every upsert, rather than adding a second database constraint — Postgres validates every unique constraint on every insert regardless of which one an upsert targets, so a legitimately-edited posting would have crashed the crawl instead of updating cleanly.

A cross-region database call was quietly costing 2-4 seconds per query — the instance had been provisioned on the wrong continent from where every request originated. Migrating it closer cut that to 50-140ms. Separately, a library's params argument silently replaced a URL's existing query string instead of merging with it, dropping a hard-coded filter from one source's request — the call still came back 200 OK with valid JSON, just the wrong data entirely; nothing about the response looked like a failure, only checking actual field values against expectations caught it.

The deepest one: Gemini's structured output silently omits fields it decides are extra work under batch load, even when the schema marks them required. That single quirk cascaded into a second bug weeks later — a validated job's experience level would get silently overwritten back to "unclear" by a routine re-crawl, and a well-meaning idempotency guard on the enrichment agent (skip anything already enriched once) made that regression permanently invisible to every future pass. 227 previously-correct rows were stuck this way before the guard condition was rethought entirely, from "has this ever been enriched" to "is it unclear right now."
## Current status

498 active sources across a dozen ATS integrations and aggregator feeds, 624 relevant postings surfaced after filtering out of roughly 11,700 raw rows kept for filter tuning, and India-region coverage nearly 6x'd over two expansion passes. Not yet deployed — Dockerfiles exist for all three services but nothing runs on Cloud Run yet, there's no scheduler so the crawl is run manually, and there's no auth in front of the dashboard, which is fine for local-only use for now.

title: Cloak402
tagline: Privacy-Preserving Orchestration Layer for AI Agents

galleryCaptions./images/projects/cloak402/Cloak402-UI.we: GhostFare — the privacy-first travel agent demo
Privacy console — full ephemeral-wallet event log

architectureCaptions./images/projects/cloak402/Cloak402-probl: The privacy problem vs. the Cloak402 solution

summary: A privacy-preserving orchestration layer that lets AI agents transact on-chain without leaking the human behind them.
description: The rise of AI agents has introduced a massive privacy loophole: agents that keep secrets. When an AI agent interacts with Web3 protocols or traditional APIs — flight searches, DeFi trades, hotel bookings — on your behalf, it emits a massive amount of metadata. Even without a persistent account, every API call, x402 payment, or contract interaction leaves a trail: observers can deanonymize the human behind the agent through on-chain graph analysis (clustering funding flows and gas sources) and off-chain logs (IP addresses, request headers, timing correlations).

Cloak402 solves this by acting as a privacy-preserving orchestration layer for AI agents. Using an autonomous travel-booking agent as a real-world implementation, it proves agents can carry out complex, multi-step commerce without doxxing the user.
Relationship anonymity via ephemeral wallets: instead of a single hot wallet, Cloak402 generates a fresh, single-use keypair in memory for every API call.

Breaking the funding graph: a naive ephemeral wallet is useless if funded directly by the user, so CloakPool — an intermediate shared pool — breaks the on-chain link between the user's main funding wallet and the ephemeral payment addresses.

Defeating heuristics: to prevent clustering, funding amounts are randomized in 0.03–0.09 USDC bands with a 1.5–6 second timing jitter, breaking the correlation between off-chain API logs and on-chain settlements.

Policy-driven disclosure puts the human back in control. In the travel-agent demo, OpenClaw enforces strict disclosure policies: searching for flights happens with absolute anonymity, while booking one selectively discloses only the minimum required data — name and email — with the financial footprint kept hidden throughout.

The result: anyone can use AI agents for sensitive tasks — from booking travel to executing private DeFi strategies — without letting service providers, MEV searchers, or on-chain sleuths build a profile on them.
## Challenges I ran into

The "naive ephemeral wallet" trap: generating a fresh viem private key for every API call looked sufficient at first, but it only achieved credential minimization, not anonymity — a trivial on-chain graph analysis could still link every ephemeral wallet back to the control wallet that was funding it for gas and x402 payments. Fixing this meant pivoting the architecture to add CloakPool as a foundational layer: routing funds through a shared pool and randomizing USDC top-ups between 0.03 and 0.09 USDC broke the 1:1 on-chain funding link.

Off-chain timing correlations: even with the funding graph broken, an observer watching the mempool and the API provider's HTTP logs could match the timestamp of a flight-search request to the timestamp of the x402 settlement, since agents execute tasks fast enough for the two to line up almost exactly. The fix was a ghostPay privacy wrapper that introduces randomized timing jitter — 1.5 to 6 seconds — before fulfilling the x402 payment, decorrelating request timing from on-chain execution.

Taming the LLM agent's urge to share data: LLMs naturally want to pass everything they know into a tool call, and early on OpenClaw would accidentally leak passenger identities during the anonymous flight-search phase just because the user had given their name earlier in the chat. Fixing it took strict, code-level separation between tools — distinct search_flights.ts and book_flight.ts CLI tools plus rigorous skill-level rules in SKILL.md that prohibit the LLM from passing PII into the search tool — backed by middleware that drops any payload violating the policy before the x402 payment ever fires.

Managing the ephemeral lifecycle: orchestrating a wallet's creation, funding, x402 handshake, data retrieval, and memory wipe within a single synchronous HTTP request cycle was prone to race conditions, especially against testnet RPC limits. The ghostPay.ts wrapper was hardened to handle those async steps robustly, so even if a step fails — like an airline API timeout — the ephemeral private key is still guaranteed to be destroyed rather than left as a dangling hot wallet.

title: PriceFlow
summary: Real-time pricing service with Python ETL pipelines feeding analytics into BigQuery.
description: Built Python ETL pipelines using Pandas, PyArrow and Apache Spark to process transactional data, store it as columnar Parquet, and load analytical datasets into Google BigQuery.
Developed the real-time pricing service in Java Spring Boot, automating price optimisation based on inventory, demand and competitor pricing, using Apache Kafka and Redis.
Implemented price-prediction models with Scikit-learn and XGBoost, with the stack containerised using Docker over MySQL.
